articles.title_orig: Nvidia earnings live: Nvidia to report Q3 results after the bell with Colette Kress to host first call as interim CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia earnings live: Nvidia to report Q3 results after the bell with Colette Kress to host first call as interim CEO
articles.content_orig:
Home Depot on Tuesday announced its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the company, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.
Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.
Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said.
"I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession plan."
McPhail has been with the company since 2005, holding multiple executive roles.
"We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.
He said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.
Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.
Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results.
The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The company said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.
Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
The company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.
Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period.
"We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail said on the call with analysts.
In the third quarter, the company said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.
The company said it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth.
For the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase.
Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's China data center curb advances despite Amazon, Google, Meta lobbying
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's China data center curb advances despite Amazon, Google, Meta lobbying
articles.content_orig:
Fears that artificial intelligence could trigger an economy-wide surge in layoffs persist, even as a recent backlash against the technology and supporting infrastructure threatens to complicate its ongoing buildout.
Widespread job cuts have emerged as a central concern now AI has become increasingly integrated into the economy, given its ability to automate certain tasks and potentially entire roles. Some research has linked AI to an increase in layoff announcements, and several high-profile companies have cited the technology when announcing major job cuts in 2026.
Economists at Goldman Sachs say an “AI-driven layoff wave” has yet to materialize but could still be on the horizon. In their recently published 2027 U.S. outlook, cited by Fortune , the economists said they expect a “slightly softer low-hire, low-fire form of full employment” to persist through next year, before “AI displacement begins to have a larger impact in subsequent years.”
This comes as opposition to AI—in part fueled by employment fears—continues to gather momentum. Concerns about data centers , their electricity usage and water consumption have become a prominent political issue this year, with some viewing the backlash as a potential obstacle to the rapid expansion of AI and its impact on the labor market.
Data centers and the AI buildout became a central issue in some state and local races ahead of the 2026 midterms , serving as a proxy for broader affordability concerns. This created electoral difficulties for some candidates who had supported data-center expansion, while voters also backed measures restricting development. According to J.P. Morgan Asset Management, 40 of 41 local ballot measures involving data centers went against development.
In a post-election analysis , Nicol Turner Lee and Darrell M. West of the Brookings Institution wrote that the results “may lead to more policy shifts around data center development and the broader tech sector itself.”
Researchers have also explored how public opposition and regulatory restrictions could slow AI adoption and potentially limit its impact on employment.
In an analysis for the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE), Era Dabla-Norris and Anton Korinek contrasted a “runaway scenario” involving widespread job displacement with one in which “regulatory friction” and “public skepticism” prevent ubiquitous AI adoption and keep labor market effects “manageable.”
Following the midterms, J.P. Morgan global market strategist Stephanie Aliaga wrote that “the AI buildout was on the ballot this year, and it lost.”
“Building out AI infrastructure was already a massive undertaking, with significant hurdles around power, permitting and financing,” she continued. “Growing political resistance adds to the difficulty, potentially bringing longer negotiations, higher costs and further delays.”
However, she added that pre-election efforts to slow the buildout had either been temporary or “struggled to advance.”
The latest monthly layoff figures from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas show that AI has been widely cited as a reason for job cuts this year. Through October, the technology had been cited in 121,401 announced job cuts, around 20 percent of the year's total, making it the second-most cited reason behind economic conditions, which accounted for 130,531. The report also records 1,265 AI-cited cuts in October alone.
However, some experts are skeptical that AI will cause catastrophic disruption to the labor market .
“Right now, AI looms large as technology that can automate workflows and replace workers, but it often seems like it is being used as a convenient boogey-man that CEOs use to justify the cuts they want to make to increase shareholder value,” Kate Fortmueller, an associate professor at Georgia State University who researches labor in the film and television industries, told Newsweek in early November.
According to an October report from TIAA, AI is “adding a new layer of uncertainty to retirement readiness,” alongside rising costs and increasing longevity. Of those surveyed, 40 percent said they considered AI in the workplace a threat to their retirement plans, rising to 51 percent among Gen Z respondents .
Goldman Sachs economists have also pointed to previous recessions as a warning of how technological change can affect employment.
“History also suggests that the full consequences of AI for the labor market might not become apparent until a recession hits,” they said. “In past recessions, employment of workers in routine occupations has dropped sharply—especially when they followed productivity booms—and did not recover after.”
Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here .
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton and Rhian Morgan .

articles.title_orig: China, Canada expand tariff relief after Carney-Xi meeting
articles.title_zh: China, Canada expand tariff relief after Carney-Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
Canada and China have agreed to cut tariffs on more goods, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney continues to look to decrease his country’s dependence on the United States amid President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
Meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday, Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping announced new tariff remissions, building on an agreement they made in January to open up trade and start to repair a strained diplomatic relationship.
China will offer tariff relief on about 400 million Canadian dollars ($280m) worth of Canadian exports, including frozen pork and seafood, said a statement from Carney’s office.
Canada, in exchange, will keep tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products in place for another two years, and add remissions to another 32 steel and aluminium items that Canada doesn’t have enough of.
Xi said stronger ties served both countries’ interests and supported global stability and prosperity.
“This is the right choice,” he said.
Carney praised the greater predictability in the relationship and said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of increasing exports to China by 50 percent by the end of the decade.
Under the January agreement, Canada lowered its 100 percent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 percent, allowing an initial 49,000 vehicles into the country each year. That cap is set to rise to 70,000 over five years.
In return, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products and recently extended relief for canola meal, peas, lobster and crab for another two years.
The deal comes a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if talks with Washington fail to hold together the closely integrated North American auto industry.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia on Monday. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”
The comments prompted a backlash from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro, who responded by asking whether Carney was threatening to “play China off the US”.
“This is offensive in the extreme,” he said, adding that Carney should be more worried that China would “eat Canada alive”.
Carney has made looking to markets beyond the US a central part of his economic strategy, as Trump’s tariffs hit Canadian industries, including auto manufacturing, as well as steel and aluminium.
Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down in August , but Carney said on Saturday that he’d spoken with Trump and senior officials, and that while differences remained, there was progress towards a possible deal.
He also met with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday, with both countries reaffirming their commitment to renew the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement , according to Carney’s office.
One year after Carney visited Mexico, during which they launched a strategic partnership, the two leaders agreed to keep expanding bilateral trade and investment. They also highlighted a 19-percent increase in merchandise trade in the first nine months of this year, compared with the same period last year.

articles.title_orig: Latin American leaders get face time with China at APEC Summit 2026
articles.title_zh: Latin American leaders get face time with China at APEC Summit 2026
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenes
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Stalled arms sales for now
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
China expands coast guard role in pressure on Taiwan
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”

articles.title_orig: Dow drops 900 points, Nasdaq hits lowest since April on Nvidia earnings angst, NSA outage concern: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow drops 900 points, Nasdaq hits lowest since April on Nvidia earnings angst, NSA outage concern: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares slipped on Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell.
Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday.
The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.title_zh: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook has refused, through her attorneys, to testify next month before a Trump administration panel evaluating her dismissal, calling the process unfair and predetermined.
This refusal prolongs the conflict between the White House and Cook's lawyers over her attendance before the committee, which officials originally demanded for Nov. 6.
Administration officials insist she address allegations of mortgage fraud in 2021 before joining the Fed's board, charges she denies.
President Donald Trump has tried to fire Cook since August 2025, with Cook arguing the president's actions threaten the central bank's independence and reflect his desire to force lower borrowing costs.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence," Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf.
The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations "appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook."
In June, the Supreme Court stopped Trump from ousting Cook as litigation regarding the dismissal continues, ruling that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design."
Trump officials have threatened to hold the hearing without Cook, stating in a Nov. 3 letter that the three-member committee "reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you" for not appearing.
The unusual "committee of inquiry" formed by the White House features Kevin Hassett, Trump’s chief economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s nominee for Labor Secretary.
The Supreme Court noted in a June ruling footnote that Trump could try again to dismiss her if provided adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee represents an attempt to meet those terms.
Under law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a governor "for cause," though the Supreme Court did not decide if Cook’s actions met that benchmark. The committee will recommend whether cause exists to dismiss her, the White House said.
When asked at an Oct. 28 press conference if he or the Fed would join the proceeding, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said, "not to my knowledge."

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (Â£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
Putin (centre) personally opened the Crimean Bridge by driving a lorry over it in May 2018
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
Images show the damage to the Crimean Bridge from the overnight attack
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Watch: BBC reports from Kyiv bridge hit by Russian attack
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: Russian military plane crashes killing all 19 on board
articles.title_zh: Russian military plane crashes killing all 19 on board
articles.content_orig:
CCTV footage posted on social media, verified by Reuters and in part by the BBC, appears to shows the plane crash
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.
CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street falters ahead of Nvidia earnings, Anthropic debut
articles.title_zh: Wall Street falters ahead of Nvidia earnings, Anthropic debut
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares slipped on Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell.
Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday.
The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Sean Duffy’s attacks on past FAA ground stop resurface
articles.title_zh: Sean Duffy’s attacks on past FAA ground stop resurface
articles.content_orig:
Nearly four years before facing a nationwide FAA ground stop as transportation secretary himself, Sean Duffy criticized his predecessor in the job, then-Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, over a similar disruption in 2023, blaming incompetent leadership and misplaced “woke” priorities.
Duffy also questioned whether additional funding was needed to fix the problems, something he now says his department desperately needs.
A former Republican congressman and Fox News contributor at the time, Duffy made the comments during two Fox News appearances where he attacked the Biden administration for saying it potentially needed more money to update FAA infrastructure. Duffy also repeatedly mocked Buttigieg for taking paternity leave after adopting twins in 2021 - more than a year before the outage – and compared it with his own experience raising nine children where he boasted that he only took just “two days” off after each birth.
“They got billions of dollars, the FAA did, over COVID,” Duffy said on Fox News i n January 2023. “And now they’re gonna come back and say, ‘We want even more money to fix this crisis that we weren’t able to handle when, you know, for what, three hours in the morning aircraft couldn’t, couldn’t fly.’”
“I don’t know that it’s more money,” he added. “I think it’s just having competent people in leadership and throughout the building that can make the organization function.”
The comments stand in sharp contrast to how Duffy has talked about last week’s ground stop, which he has blamed entirely on failed, aging equipment he says won’t be fully fixed without an additional $50 billion. Whereas in 2023, Duffy repeatedly blamed the political leadership of the Biden administration, specifically Buttigieg, for that ground stop.
Asked on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday whether he accepted responsibility for the latest outage, Duffy acknowledged his role overseeing the FAA but pointed to the aging infrastructure he inherited.
“Of course, I’m the secretary,” Duffy said. “But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me…I take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations.”
Duffy said the FAA was still operating with systems dating back decades and argued that the billions already approved by Congress was insufficient to complete the necessary upgrades.
Friday’s ground stop occurred after a telecommunications outage caused instability in radar data and communications with aircraft, prompting the FAA to halt departures nationwide for more than four hours. Duffy told CNN the problem appeared to emerge during routine work by contractor L3Harris to replace aging copper wire telecommunications infrastructure with fiber-optic technology.
Officials are investigating whether mistakes during that work or faulty equipment caused the failure.
The January 2023 ground stop occurred after an outage of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system, which provides pilots with critical safety information before flights. The outage prompted the agency to temporarily halt domestic departures nationwide for several hours. Investigators later determined that contractors had accidentally deleted files while working on the system’s databases.
In the hours following the January 2023 ground stop, Duffy took aim at Buttigieg during an appearance on Fox News’ America Reports , mocking his paternity leave and questioning his ability to lead the department through a crisis.
Buttigieg took approximately eight weeks of paternity leave, from mid-August to mid-October 2021, after he and his husband welcomed premature newborn twins, but the department said he was mostly offline for just the first four weeks.
“I think if Pete would stay home, go back on paternity vacation, maybe this could all just run itself,” Duffy said. “It seems when Pete shows up, things go wrong.”
“He can’t lead us through anything and doesn’t know what the problem was,” Duffy added, repeatedly and incorrectly saying Buttigieg took a “four month” leave.
During the segment, Fox News aired a live press conference where Buttigieg pledged to investigate the root cause of the outage, examine why backup systems had failed and identify what upgrades were needed to prevent another disruption.
Two days later, during a January 13 appearance on Fox News’ The Faulkner Focus , Duffy again criticized Buttigieg, accusing him of failing to identify and address weaknesses in the FAA’s aging infrastructure.
“Leadership means you look at the systems and agency in which you run, where do we have some shortcomings and where do we have to do upgrades? Pete Buttigieg hasn’t done that,” Duffy said. “Why wasn’t the money put into upgrading the FAA systems?”
In a statement to CNN, a Transportation Department spokesperson defended Duffy’s record and attacked Buttigieg.
“To compare Secretary Duffy’s record – which includes securing a $12.5 billion downpayment to begin updating our country’s air traffic control network after decades of neglect and launching a successful gamer campaign to supercharge ATC hiring – to a failed political hack like Pete Buttigieg is laughable.”
When asked by CNN to comment on Duffy’s criticisms, a spokesperson for Buttigieg pointed to a social media post on Monday, in which Buttigieg cited his own record, saying, “As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived. We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in years.”
Duffy’s own congressional record on FAA funding is mixed.
In January 2019, during the government shutdown, Duffy joined 179 other Republicans in voting against a Democratic-backed spending bill aimed at reopening transportation and housing agencies. The legislation included funding for FAA operations and air traffic control modernization, along with numerous provisions unrelated to aviation.
But Duffy also voted for FAA funding and reauthorization measures in 2012 , 2013 and 2018 . A 2025 PolitiFact review found no public statements from Duffy at the time explaining his opposition to the 2019 bill. When asked about the vote six years later, a Duffy spokesperson told PolitiFact the legislation would have provided only a small increase in FAA funding.
A review of available archived pages from Duffy’s congressional website found no statements addressing national air traffic control modernization or FAA appropriations, with the FAA-related announcements identified in the review focusing on federal grants for airports in his Wisconsin district.
A separate search of Duffy’s appearances in the Internet Archive’s television news archive identified no discussions of FAA modernization before his criticism of Buttigieg following the January 2023 ground stop.
Duffy’s criticism of Buttigieg for taking time away from the job after his children were born also comes after Duffy spent part of his first two years as transportation secretary participating in a reality series with his own family.
Duffy and his wife, Rachel Campos-Duffy, and their nine children filmed “The Great American Road Trip” over a seven-month period, according to CNN’s previous reporting. The six-episode series, released on the Department of Transportation’s YouTube channel in August, followed the family through seven states as part of an effort to promote travel for the nation’s 250th anniversary.
A spokesperson for the Department of the Transportation defended Duffy’s participation in the series saying, “The series was filmed over the course of many months in small, one day or two stops.”
This story has been updated.

articles.title_orig: Take-Two lays off Firaxis employees on eve of Grand Theft Auto VI launch
articles.title_zh: Take-Two lays off Firaxis employees on eve of Grand Theft Auto VI launch
articles.content_orig:
Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM franchises of computer strategy games, last week laid off about a third of its staff, totaling around 60 people. That’s according to a recent report in Bloomberg.
The report cites people “familiar with the cuts,” saying that the flagship game the studio is currently working on, a new entry in the XCOM series, “has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone.” The departures also include the studio head, Heather Hazen.
A Firaxis spokesperson released the following statement:
Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.
The storied studio has had a rough run of things of late. Its most recent game, Civilization VII , launched to solid enough sales but divided players in terms of reception. Players have long criticized new Civilization titles for being barebones compared to immediate predecessors that have seen multiple post-launch updates and expansions, but the response was sharper this time.
The game has found more fans in recent months , but a portion of the Civilization audience will likely never fully warm to it due to its ages system—a design choice that partially solved many long-standing pacing problems, but at the cost of altering the core experience.
Before that, Firaxis worked on Marvel’s Midnight Suns , which had a more positive reception in terms of sentiment but does not seem to have sold as many units as the company had hoped. Now, with the new XCOM title facing challenges, that’s three troubled games in a row.
To top it off, most of Firaxis’ direct competitors in the strategy game market are much leaner and not beholden to a major publisher. (The publisher for the Civilization franchise is 2K Games, which lives under the same company that publishes the soon-to-launch Grand Theft Auto VI .)
The industry at large has seen widespread layoffs and studio closures over the past few years. There’s no single reason for that; rather, there are numerous factors, including contraction after COVID-era over-investment, increased competition, changes in leadership culture at major publishers, and larger economic factors beyond the scope of just the games industry.

articles.title_zh: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
articles.content_orig:
After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, now it’s Apple customers who are facing technical issues.
The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.
Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.
On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone , which is likely related to these ongoing issues.
Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues .
Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches.
So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.
Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg ), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.
After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com),  Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program.

articles.title_orig: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong says rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are ‘extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on those involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank .
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong , said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements. The statement did not name the company.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”
Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the UK on the sanctions.
“We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions.
“We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.”
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australia sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had in the past.
after newsletter promotion
“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.

articles.title_orig: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
articles.title_zh: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
articles.content_orig:
Iran fired drones across the Persian Gulf on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom as Tehran resumed strikes on its Arab neighbors after a roughly two-month lull.
After issuing an alert of the incoming fire, Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the “treacherous Iranian aerial attacks.”
The attack came after the U.S. military’s Central Command confirmed that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group had arrived in the region. The move adds a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the American presence as U.S. President Donald Trump keeps his options open for his next move in the war, which began nearly nine months ago.
The combined U.S. naval assets in the Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel conducted joint strikes on Iran to launch the war on Feb. 28 — the presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn’t comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region or replace the Washington, which had been redeployed from the Asia-Pacific region to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln amid concerns of its lengthy deployment.
The Washington itself has now been deployed for around six months.
Iran’s attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said that they were done in retaliation.
“Continued aggression against the country’s airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran will not go unanswered,” Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
The U.S. military didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the recent attacks.
With negotiations stagnating on bringing an end to the war, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar, the latest military developments have further complicated prospects for a negotiated settlement, said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, in an analysis posted to X.
As the U.S. mulls whether to resume all-out military attacks on Iran or to intensify its blockade to further sap strength from Iran’s economy, Iranian leaders will also now be weighing whether “breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation,” Azizi wrote.
“In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again,” he said. “It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation.”
The attacks on the American facilities in Bahrain are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient with the waiting game as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
“Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation,” Bruchmann told The Associated Press. “Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn’t overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet.”
Iranian officials have termed the current situation “no war, no peace” and vowed that it must be brought to an end.
Tehran has said that it’s open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran’s economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic “security crisis.” He said that the strikes on Bahrain were meant “to prevent the gradual expansion of enemy operations and to impose costs on its military infrastructure.”
Iran has also continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas.
Before the war, ships had freely passed through the key waterway, carrying about a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas. Since then, Iran has held a tight grip on the strait and only a fraction of the peacetime shipping traffic has been able to pass through, despite U.S. efforts to provide escorts.
On Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said that a tanker was reportedly attacked twice north of Oman, and that the second strike caused a fire on board.
Iran’s Fars news agency also reported that two ships were struck by mines in the strait, causing them to catch fire. It wasn’t immediately clear whether one was the incident reported by the British military’s UKMTO.
In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route, which connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea, after a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government retreated on the weekend in a setback to the anti-Houthi coalition.
Those government-allied forces are now fortifying their defenses in areas leading to the southern city of Aden, which serves as an interim capital of the internationally recognized government, two Yemeni military officials said.
Their efforts are focused on deploying more troops and equipment in and around the district of Tur al-Baha in the southern province of Lahij, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after images showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
VIDEO: Driverless Waymo tries to bypass CHP traffic break on SF freeway
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told ABC7 Eyewitness News.
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026 , Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says these new restrictions went into effect on November 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
MORE: Study finds lower crash rate for Waymo vehicles in San Francisco
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again Monday.
"I used to use it all the time and now it's like ehh I'll walk, or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.title_zh: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said .
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.
The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.
This was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced issues with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.
This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.
There are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the company said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.
“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the company said . “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”
If Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the New Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

articles.title_orig: The first pill to slow Alzheimer’s could come from an unexpected place
articles.title_zh: The first pill to slow Alzheimer’s could come from an unexpected place
articles.content_orig:
Laura has led award-winning coverage on the NHS, medical science breakthroughs, and public health policy across the UK for The Telegraph. Her reporting can be found on X: @lauradonnlee
A Viagra-like drug could slow Alzheimer’s disease, its manufacturer’s trial results suggest.
The once-daily pill slowed decline by 31 per cent over a year among patients who were not already taking standard Alzheimer’s medicines.
The benefit was in 604 of 1,535 patients. Across the whole trial, researchers could not establish a significant benefit.
The findings of the international trial, whose lead investigator was based at Stanford University, were presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston.
The experimental treatment, called AR1001, contains mirodenafil, a drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction.
It belongs to the same family of medicines as Viagra, but is a different drug, and the findings do not establish that Viagra itself can treat Alzheimer’s.
Researchers believe AR1001 could protect brain cells by acting on several processes involved in Alzheimer’s, including inflammation and changes to the tau protein.
Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said: “These are very encouraging results, marking an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments.”
She said the drug was particularly interesting because it was a tablet that worked differently from existing treatments, targeting several processes involved in brain function.
The trial involved 1,535 people with early Alzheimer’s across 13 countries, including Britain.
Participants received either AR1001 or a dummy pill, with researchers tracking their memory, thinking and ability to manage everyday tasks over a year.
The benefit was seen among 604 patients who were not already taking standard Alzheimer’s medicines. In this group, those taking AR1001 deteriorated 31 per cent more slowly than those given the dummy pill.
However, when researchers looked at all 1,535 patients together, including those already taking other Alzheimer’s medicines, they could not establish a significant benefit.
Dr Scales said: “The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group.”
It is not yet clear why the drug worked for patients who were not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines.
These included memantine and medicines known as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which are used to treat Alzheimer’s symptoms.
Dr Richard Oakley, associate director for research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society, said: “These topline results are an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms. “It’s fantastic to see research and clinical trials unlocking promising new ways to target Alzheimer’s Disease. AR1001 takes a novel approach, relaxing blood vessels to increase blood flow to the brain. And unlike other disease-modifying treatments that have shown benefit in late-stage trials, it is taken as a once-a-day tablet, which could make treatment simpler.”
Researchers measured deterioration using an 18-point scale assessing memory, judgment and everyday abilities.
Over the year, patients taking AR1001 in the smaller group deteriorated by 0.44 points less than those given the dummy pill.
This represented a 31 per cent reduction in the rate of decline, rather than an improvement in patients’ existing symptoms.
Other tests of thinking and daily functioning also favoured the drug, although several differences were not statistically significant.
Tests of spinal fluid provided evidence that the drug was acting on its intended biological target within the brain and nervous system.
AR1001 blocks an enzyme called PDE5, increasing a chemical signal involved in several processes that researchers believe could help protect brain cells.
Dr Sharon Sha, chief of the Memory Disorders Division at Stanford University and global principal investigator of the trial, said the results among patients not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines were encouraging, as was the drug’s safety record.
She said further research was needed to understand its effects.
“The work of POLARIS-AD is another step towards filling an unmet need in Alzheimer’s disease in which patients need more options for treatment,” she said.
AriBio, the company developing AR1001, plans to discuss the findings with US regulators, a potential step towards seeking approval for the pill as an Alzheimer’s treatment.
Dr David Greeley of AriBio, who led the drug’s earlier Phase 2 trial, said the findings were “very encouraging”.
He said: “If approved, this oral drug would broaden patients’ options.”
He added: “Further evaluation is needed, but our goal is meaningful treatment that not only helps patients but that can be realistically afforded, received and sustained.”
The company said the drug was generally well tolerated, with serious adverse events reported in similar proportions of the treatment and placebo groups.
Diarrhoea, falls and dizziness were among the most common adverse events. About 5 per cent stopped the drug because of adverse events, compared with 2 per cent receiving a placebo.
Most participants who completed the first year entered an extension study, in which everyone received the drug. It is expected to finish next year.
Dr Scales said: “We look forward to seeing whether these benefits are sustained over the longer term.”
Researchers said they closely monitored “unwanted sexual behaviour” during the trial and no significant signal had been reported.

articles.title_orig: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.title_zh: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.content_orig:
Apple said an internal update was to blame for a major outage on Nov. 17 that hit its App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay and other software, with thousands of users reporting problems online.
In a statement to USA TODAY, Apple said it was working to fix the affected systems, and services are expected to return to normal soon.
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible," the company said.
Apple, on its System Status page , confirmed outages on App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device, as well as issues with iCloud Account & Sign In. The company told Bloomberg the problems weren't caused by a cyberattack.
According to outage tracker Downdetector, reports of issues with Apple Pay began to spike at around 11:40 a.m. ET with a peak of reports at around 12:15 p.m. ET. Outage reports for iCloud also started to surge just before noon ET, though reports on Downdetector don't reflect every user experiencing a problem. Those reports had dropped significantly by mid-afternoon.
The Apple software issues came on the heels of a major banking outage on Nov. 16 that stemmed from Chase Bank. It also impacted Wells Fargo, Bank of America, online payment platform Zelle and other institutions.
Last week, a communications outage disrupted air traffic across the United States, and a Microsoft outage prevented many from checking their Outlook email and accessing Microsoft 365 services like Teams and Word.
