articles.title_orig: Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
articles.title_zh: Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
articles.content_orig:
Three strongman leaders over age 70, 90% of the world’s nuclear weapons, two ongoing wars, one room, and no specific agenda. What could possibly go wrong?
What Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will discuss during their unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday is far from concrete. But that is perhaps the point. A high-level summit like this would usually establish clear outcomes ahead of time, and be the culmination of months of intense planning and signalling.
But whatever preceded the Shenzhen meeting matters little with the inclusion of a wild card like Trump. Nuclear non-proliferation was flagged as a main focus, though little progress is expected – to say nothing of “safeguarding world peace,” another agenda item according to China. Then suddenly, Trump mentioned Iran, Ukraine, Nvidia, and even floated a meeting with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
It’s not abnormal for world leaders to go off script. Yet it has rarely been as risky as it will be Thursday. Especially when it comes to Ukraine.
Trump referred to Europe’s longest ongoing war Monday with both a slip of a tongue and sarcasm. He called Ukraine “my favorite subject” and added, “Ukraine’s losing – Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month” – almost edging Russia’s horrific losses out of his sentence. Ukraine is for Trump the irritant that got itself invaded, hasn’t accepted his hurried and compromising peace, and is always losing.
The Shenzhen meeting is a risky moment not because Kyiv and its European allies will suddenly buckle under whatever declarations emerge; they have grown sufficiently inured to Washington’s fickle nature. The danger is in Trump’s desire to be liked by powerful authoritarians, what is agreed to in private, and how that informs Putin’s confidence and Xi’s perception of Trump’s mental health.
Putin has, for free, got his moment on the world stage, allowing him to present Russia, for a day, as the global superpower it once was, rather than the one it is brutally struggling to become again.
Anxiety among European officials is palpable. “Trump listens to the last person he talks to, so that will be a driver for what he says,” said one European official speaking to CNN on the condition of anonymity. A European diplomat said it was: “Hard to see anything good on European security to come out of this meeting.”
Another senior European official said the optics of the trilateral were “of course awful for us,” but was less concerned a wider deal would be struck.
The first official called the meeting a “Putin dream,” ushering in his rehabilitation on the world stage, and added a key issue for Trump would be “who stands in the middle of the big boys takeaway picture.”
That picture of the three leaders after their meeting will speak a thousand words about Western decline. The man who invaded Ukraine unprovoked nearly five years ago, his bankroller in chief, and the US president who has reversed decades of US policy to pressure Kyiv to accept a bad deal, through limiting military aid.
A key risk is Trump agreeing with a Russian narrative, or fictional presentation of the frontline facts, and feeling obliged to adhere to a deal he has hurriedly made with the two strongmen he not-so-secretly admires.
Many of the European officials CNN spoke to harbor distant hopes that Beijing may emerge as a good-faith arbiter in the war. It is a view born of Xi’s apparent pressure on Putin to curtail nuclear saber-rattling , China’s stopping short of the full-scale arming of Russia during the war, and Beijing’s ambition to become the global superpower that can enforce effective change.
But this rosy view overlooks how urgently China needs Moscow to not lose this war, to prevent another key ally from suffering humiliation, and how the US has ridden roughshod over Iran and Venezuela this year – two Chinese allies whose degradation Beijing might like to see avenged by the collective West suffering a defeat in Ukraine.
The past month has delivered repeated blows to Ukraine and European NATO countries, dressed in the guise of the US peace process, led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and friend Steve Witkoff, two envoys who have limited diplomatic experience and even less diplomatic successes to their names. First, Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, wiping away years of sanctions and opening the door to the replenishing of the Kremlin’s war chest. Then followed the mysterious stoppages in US intelligence sharing and Starshield services – vital to the nightly defense of Ukraine from Russian missiles – that the White House appears to have suggested either didn’t happen or shouldn’t have.
In a Kremlin meeting last month, Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian” after he released retired American teacher and US military veteran Stephen Hubbard.
Then Kushner, after meeting Putin’s envoy in DC, recast the peace process as a bid for a new European security infrastructure, pandering to the Kremlin narrative that the real belligerent is NATO next door - and not Russia, who invaded one neighbour, Georgia in 2008, and another, Ukraine, twice in 2014 and 2022.
After further Starshield restrictions were placed on Ukraine during a peace summit, Kushner flew to Moscow hoping Putin would “give his blessing” to Europe joining the trilateral peace talks. He emerged saying Putin had done so, only to be flatly contradicted by the Kremlin. And finally, Kushner appears to have suggested NATO-type security guarantees if Ukraine gives up the rest of the Donbas region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
And, this is just the stuff that is publicly known. It is not too far-fetched to see the Shenzhen summit as the pinnacle of Trump’s settling into Moscow’s orbit. His actions in public show no other course. He even suggested Putin could have been “a lot tougher” on Ukraine, a statement that can only nod to Russia’s nuclear arsenal, given its nightly exhausting of its conventional armaments into Ukraine’s skies.
This will not be a feared Yalta 2.0, in which global powers carve up the world. The first Yalta summit in 1945 divided the world after the worst conflict in its history, between three victors whose empires either crumbled or bloomed afterwards.
Different men will attend Shenzhen. Trump and Putin are fighting different and failing wars of choice, and are the aging embodiment of their nations’ waning power. Xi has overseen a brutal, staggeringly efficient and swift rise of a global tech superpower, but still flinches away from conflict in his own potential war of choice – the invasion of Taiwan.
History had no choice but to listen to Truman, Stalin and Churchill after World War II. It might choose to tune out Shenzhen.
But the damage need not come in the form of Trump parroting Kremlin talking points when he emerges. Or Putin being given a space on the world stage for his false historical lectures on Russian victimhood and supremacy. Or Xi – probably the largest-scale authoritarian in history – appearing to be the reasonable, calm one.
The gift to Moscow is in how little opposition Putin will feel. The two most powerful men in the world are likely to give him an easy ride in private, and not demand an immediate ceasefire or durable peace in Ukraine. Pressure will instead be focused on Ukrainian and European concessions. The peace process may suffer yet another curiously pro-Russian reset that buys the Kremlin months more to try and seize tiny pockets of the Donbas, or let Ukrainian mothers and children suffer through another freezing winter.
There is little time left for these aging leaders – Xi is 73, Putin is 74 and Trump is 80 – to change the world. Perhaps this is just a blip in the autocratic curve of history. But the ticking clock makes the remaining two years of this US presidency particularly perilous.

articles.title_orig: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
articles.title_zh: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
articles.content_orig:
By MELISSA KOENIG, US REPORTER and ASSOCIATED PRESS
Published: 17:12 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 08:04 EST, 17 November 2026
United Airlines flights across the United States were grounded on Monday night, just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to ground all flights nationwide.
The airline announced on social media that it was experiencing a 'widespread system outage' as it apologized to customers 'for the inconvenience.'
'We're aware of the widespread system and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible,' it posted on X.
'We appreciate your patience while we work through this,' the airline added, urging anyone with scheduled flights to keep checking their flight status on the app.
The post has since been deleted, as a spokesperson for the airline told the Daily Mail that the issue has been resolved.
'While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,' the spokesperson said, adding: 'There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.'
The update came after frustrated travelers took to social media to bemoan how their flights could not take off.
'Currently stuck on the tarmac,' one X user posted, blaming it on an IT issue in which the airline 'can't clear planes for takeoff as [they] can't connect to the weight system.'
United Airlines flights across the country were grounded Monday night as the airline experienced a 'widespread system outage'
The issue comes just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to ground all flights nationwide
United Airlines said on social media its teams were 'working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible'
The outage is now the latest in a string of technical issues that have crippled businesses around the country and left airline passengers stranded for hours amid a rare nationwide ground stop.
Earlier Monday, thousands of customers with Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo also flagged being unable to log in or transfer money , according to Down Detector, a website which tracks real-time user reports.
A spokesperson for Chase told the Daily Mail the outage was caused by a technical bug.
'Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,' they said. 'We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.'
Chase also addressed one complaint on X, telling a client: 'I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking.
'Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience.'
Wells Fargo also posted a note on its website telling customers that 'online banking isn't available right now' due to 'technical issues'.
A spokesperson for Chase later noted that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack.
'JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system - it is not cyber-related,' said spokesman Joe Evangelisti.
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
'This is not a systemic issue - other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,' he said.
Customers at three major US banks have been locked out of their accounts as Chase and Wells Fargo all experienced outages on Monday afternoon
Over 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday
A spokesman for US Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that 'clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.'
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
'An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,' the spokesman said.
Still, the outage sparked panic as it came just three days after Microsoft experienced widespread issues on Friday , leaving people unable to access Outlook, Teams and Copilot applications.
Businesses ground to a halt, healthcare providers lost contact with patients, courts lost live feeds, and governments struggled to communicate.
The suspected cause was a faulty network configuration change that resulted in numerous servers becoming unavailable, overloading the remaining infrastructure.
The FAA also issued a rare nationwide ground stop at all US airports following a major communications failure on Friday.
'What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,' Trump said on Monday of the FAA outage that forced thousands of cancelled and delayed flights over the weekend
The Air Traffic Control System Command Center (ATCSCC) said on Friday that the  halting of 3,500 US flights for five hours was 'due to extraordinary circumstances for safety reasons'.
'There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted,' the FAA said.
'Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis.'
President Donald Trump has since blamed half-century-old aviation equipment for the ground stop, which led to thousands of cancellations and travel woes for over a million passengers.
'We have old, broken equipment,' the President said Monday at the White House before departing for his trip to Asia on board the new Air Force One plane gifted to the administration by Qatari officials.
He noted that some of the equipment that went down was 55 years old.
'We essentially want to blow it up and put new in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble. What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.'
The incident marked only the second time since the 9/11 terrorist attacks that a nationwide ground stop was implemented.
The stoppage also prevented any domestic flights from taking off, resulting in one of the worst travel snarls in recent US history. It began around 3.30pm and was not lifted until around 8.20pm.
More than 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday.
It is estimated that more than one million American travelers have been impacted by the outage.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy claimed Biden-era upgrades were shoddy
The President also cast blame on his predecessor for the FAA glitch.
'The Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass. And copper, if you know anything about electrical engineering, you cannot hook up copper into glass. So a lot of money was wasted, but the equipment is very old,' Trump said.
He was referring to Biden-era upgrades to communication systems built on copper wiring that were upgraded to fiber-optic, or glass, wires.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the upgrade work was shoddy, resulting in the outage.
Trump said the upgrade was a waste of money and more cash would be needed from Congress to fully upgrade the system and prevent future issues.
'We want to make it beyond safe. We want to have the best system in the world, and for that we need Congress,' the President told reporters.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Is Willing to Return as Nvidia CEO If Board Allows It
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Is Willing to Return as Nvidia CEO If Board Allows It
articles.content_orig:
In his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO last week, Jensen Huang struck a contrite tone, saying that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence contact.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in the written statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
Huang said he had seen support from investors and employees and was willing to come back as CEO to help the company navigate "complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I  would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in the statement.
Sources told CNBC Monday that the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO.
Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO, putting together an online petition with more than 180,000 signatures.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia.
Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang, Nvidia's founder, admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had a liason with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence. Jensen Huang also reportedly had romances with employees at Nvidia.
Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. Its board of directors said on Friday that it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.
Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
Here is the entire statement from Huang:
Over the past week, I've been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry  colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the  greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life's work. Building it  into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor.  Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I  love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious  mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my  mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent  investigation.
Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my  return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

articles.title_orig: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.title_zh: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

Starting today, the Gemini app’s “tasks” feature, previously known as Spark, is now available for free users after requiring AI Pro in the past.
Google previously referred to this capability as a 24/7 personal agent before integrating directly into the main Gemini app experience in October . Above the prompt box on mobile (or below on the web), you’ll see “Chat” and “Task.” The first option is the existing chatbot, while the latter lets you “hand off even more tasks to Gemini.”
With tasks, Google’s “goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.” Google shared use cases like:
With today’s announcement, Google is emphasizing that “Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because [your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards] already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.”
Behind the scenes, Gemini tasks work in your own “hardware-isolated virtual machine” that’s sandboxed and has protections against prompt injection, while leveraging Google Safe Browsing when browsing the web.
Other safety features include having you confirm purchases and asking “clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.”
Powered by the new Hydrogen model , free Gemini tasks are available in the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

articles.title_orig: Social media algorithms are encouraging Americans to freak out about the tech outages
articles.title_zh: Social media algorithms are encouraging Americans to freak out about the tech outages
articles.content_orig:
A version of this story appeared in CNN’s Reliable Sources newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .
How do seemingly ordinary tech snafus become ominous signs of impending societal collapse?
When they’re filtered through algorithms that reward alarmism, that’s how.
There’s a lot of that happening right now. Conspiracy theories about government plots and power blackouts are cropping up after the Microsoft cloud outage, the nationwide ground stop and other recent disruptions.
My advice is simple: Don’t let the algorithms scare you. Preparedness is smart; panic is not.
So let’s try to separate what’s real from what’s reckless. What’s real: The palpable and understandable anxiety right now about a succession of tech outages. “It has been one massive tech disruption after another, and it’s putting people on edge,” Kate Bolduan said on “CNN News Central.”
People are asking if rogue AI systems, human hackers or other culprits are poking holes in the infrastructure we all take for granted. And government officials aren’t exactly assuaging the fears. “It’s fine,” President Donald Trump said glibly in response to a question about the outages on Tuesday.
Widespread distrust in Trump, his administration and other institutions makes it harder to convince people that there’s nothing more sinister going on.
But here’s the thing: Legit questions about the digital infrastructure underpinning our lives are being exploited by doomsday preppers and bad-faith actors. There are reckless comments all across Facebook and X, and conspiratorial videos all over TikTok and Instagram, that simply don’t reflect reality.
No, there wasn’t a system outage at Costco on Monday. No, there wasn’t a secret test of the electrical grid. Yes, there was a test of the Emergency Alert System, but it was totally routine and maybe just poorly timed.
Human brains are wired to look for patterns, and the endless scroll provides endless chances to find them, especially when social media influencers appear to be “just asking questions” about what’s going on.
It’s wiser to seek out sources with actual answers, rather than just questions, and to look out the window after looking down at the phone.
But let’s face it: Some people like to indulge in nightmare-scenario planning for the same reasons they enjoy disaster movies. More than one Fox News host on Monday night sounded like a full-blown prepper.
The commentary is its own fuel, causing all sorts of conspiracy thinking, including from prominent political figures. Trump confidant Laura Loomer posted tweets on Monday saying “Doesn’t everything just feel so weird?” and telling her followers to “go get cash.”
Other influencers have tried to connect dots that have no known connections — insinuating that a shadowy entity is laying the groundwork for something apocalyptic.
Conspiracy mongers like Alex Jones have been making a living by peddling these storylines for years, surely hoping that viewers will never notice that the predicted doomsday has never arrived.
So when these posts pop up in your feed, ask yourself: What could be motivating the poster? Are they trying to get me to reply (and give their account more attention) or buy something or advance a political agenda? Are they raking in affiliate fee revenue when they tell me to purchase emergency supplies, you know, just in case?
There’s a reason why it’s called “doomscrolling.” Once your favorite social media platform knows you’re paying attention to a particular topic, it delivers more and more, often distorting how significant it really is.
We each exist in a personalized media bubble. And in my bubble, at least, posters are passing the time comparing their emergency stockpiles and cracking jokes about what they’ll do if the lights go out.
My response: I’m going to put down the phone and hang up some Christmas lights.
I don’t mean to be dismissive. It’s fair to wonder whether autonomous AI agents — and the IT pros trying to counter those rogue bots — are responsible for all this tech turbulence. And it’s logical to expect further trouble, Chris Krebs, the former director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said on CNN’s “The Situation Room.”
“I believe it’s going to get better in the long run, but I would expect to see disruptions in some services over the next several months,” Krebs said. That’s partly because “we’re using AI to find vulnerabilities in software and systems, and we’re patching systems at a rate far beyond anything in the past.”
But “any time you do a patch, any time you roll an update, it can destabilize the system,” Krebs told CNN’s Pamela Brown.
While that’s going on, we have to keep a sense of perspective, in part because algorithms don’t. I noticed many X accounts on Monday wildly overstating United’s brief system outage, which affected only a small number of flights.
Monday’s outage was “so pedestrian, it’d be a non-story if not for what’s happened the last four days,” Thrifty Traveler editor Kyle Potter wrote .
Customer complaints about online banking outages might not have made news, either, if not for last week’s Microsoft and Workday cloud software outages.
And FEMA probably wouldn’t have posted a tweet saying “we’ve heard a lot of rumors” about Tuesday’s Emergency Alert System test.
This routine test had been scheduled for months (I checked), but it was already being incorporated into some of this week’s conspiracy theories.
There are “no blackouts, no secret emergencies,” FEMA tweeted. “Just our legally mandated, routine test on TV and radio at approximately 2:20 PM ET.” Officials told CNN the test went smoothly.
As for all the emergency preparedness chatter on social media, Krebs pointed out on NBC’s “Today” show that FEMA recommends having “food, water and other supplies to last for several days” in the event of an emergency.
Being prepared in the digital age also means having physical, offline copies of important documents and account numbers.
“It sounds prepperish, but it’s really not,” Krebs said. “It’s just kind of being an adult in modern society.”

articles.title_orig: Inside Microsoft’s giant Outlook outage
articles.title_zh: Inside Microsoft’s giant Outlook outage
articles.content_orig:
A bug took down Microsoft’s email services for millions around the world.
A bug took down Microsoft’s email services for millions around the world.
At 9AM last Thursday, everything seemed normal. Microsoft employees were arriving on campus, ready for a regular day of emails and meetings. But barely an hour later, one of Microsoft’s worst outages in history started to unfold, leaving employees, businesses, and many governments without access to Outlook emails for nearly 24 hours.
It all started in Switzerland, according to a source familiar with the outage. Exchange Online servers that power Outlook started to fall offline. The problem quickly spread to Mexico, and then to other countries around the world, as Microsoft’s failover systems tried to shift email traffic elsewhere. Within a couple of hours, more than 80 percent of Exchange servers were unresponsive.
Sources tell me that Microsoft marked the outage as “sev0” in its internal incident tracking system, the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Hundreds of engineers began trying to figure out what had gone wrong, and how to restore service. It’s not unusual for servers to fail under certain circumstances, but Microsoft has a variety of systems that are supposed to route traffic toward healthy servers to keep the broader system online. In this case, the failover systems did their job, but they also spread the problem.
In the early hours of the outage, engineers were analyzing crash reports, trace logs, and kernel dumps to try and find clues to the giant outage. Some servers had entered into maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads. Engineers tried to bring servers back online, but they were almost immediately overwhelmed by traffic waiting to access the servers.
Exchange servers boot up and run an OS over a network (Preboot Execution Environment), a process that allows Microsoft’s support staff and engineers to manage OS updates remotely. I understand that the sudden burst of traffic from servers being rebooted was overwhelming the systems monitoring them, causing a form of reboot loop where they kept trying and failing to come back online.
As engineers continued to hunt for the root cause, Microsoft was even struggling to roll back servers to a healthy state using its usual processes of reverting recent changes. As the outside world began to wonder if this outage was related to a cyberattack or sloppy AI coding, Microsoft’s engineers were already investigating potential attack vectors and liaising with DDoS specialists to understand whether this could have been an attack.
I’m told crash reports and logs quickly ruled out the possibility of an attack, and after recent rollbacks failed, Microsoft’s engineers began to take a closer look at the networking stack of the servers and discovered an unusual bug. It was unusual because the bug had been sitting on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers since July without any impact to servers.
“A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions,” wrote Charles Lamanna , the leader of Microsoft’s Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) team, in a post on X . The teams behind Office, Outlook, and Microsoft Teams all started reporting to Lamanna last month after the head of Office and Teams, Ryan Roslansky , left the company .
Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report describes the bug as one affecting select Windows servers “due to lock contention inside an internal Windows process.” The bug doesn’t affect regular versions of Windows since it was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.
Microsoft didn’t find the bug until this major outage, and it admits that was because of the traffic mix and hardware used in its testing labs. “The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores,” Lamanna wrote.
The bug became obvious because of two other incidents that increased load and reduced server capacity. Fifteen hours before this Outlook outage began, Microsoft Teams failed over from an alternative networking gateway to the main gateway that supports Exchange Online. “This increased the load on the networking gateway and changed its traffic patterns,” Lamanna wrote. Ordinarily this wouldn’t have been a problem, but at the same time around 14 percent of server capacity for this gateway was “out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day.”
The trifecta of a bug, Microsoft Teams failing over, and reduced server capacity all caused the network gateway to trigger the problem that had been lying dormant since July. It took Microsoft nearly 24 hours to get its Exchange servers stable again, and I’m told overlapping interventions from teams trying to fix issues complicated coordination at times.
Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call the entire time, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants. That shows you how many teams were involved with trying to find the root cause of this huge outage, which started at the peak window of traffic in the US.
“Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” Lamanna wrote. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state. Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.”
Microsoft is now working on a final post-incident review that will be published later this week. Even without that full review, it’s clear that the company will need to invest more into its testing processes to ensure that when something like this happens again, it can catch the problem a lot sooner. Outages happen daily, but this kind of cascading failure is a rare moment for Microsoft to learn from its mistakes and make sure the same sequence of events doesn’t bring down Outlook for millions of people again.

I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there.

articles.title_orig: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.
The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.
Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.
"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."
The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.
The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.
CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.
Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.
Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.
"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."
Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.
— CNBC's Phil LeBeau , Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

articles.title_orig: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.title_zh: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — When European nations said they wanted greater involvement in Ukraine peace talks , this was almost certainly not what they had in mind.
Europe has long demanded more say in negotiations to end Russia’s war , fearful of being frozen out by Washington and Moscow. They dread a deal favorable to President Vladimir Putin — who will meet President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a historic three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.
The good news for them is that the United States says it is now pushing to include Europe in the next rounds of diplomacy. The bad news, say governments, officials and foreign policy analysts, is the alarming new suggestion from Trump’s team: that the entire future of European security should be up for discussion too  — the same demand that Putin has pushed for years .
To the Russian leader, redrawing Europe’s security map means scaling back NATO’s presence, righting what he perceives as the injustices imposed on Moscow after the Soviet Union’s collapse. A succession of senior European officials have lambasted the idea, warning that Washington risks “walking into Moscow’s trap,” as Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, put it.
“This is all rather bizarre,” former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves said, summing up this sentiment in an interview with NBC News on Monday.
It’s not clear how or why the U.S. came to float a maximalist demand that Putin first made in 2021, one that was widely rejected by Western governments months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine . But in recent days, as Washington ups its pressure for a breakthrough in peace talks, Russia and the U.S. have both revived the idea.
Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and envoy, wrote Friday that talks should tackle the “broader postwar European security arrangements.”
Earlier this month, he lamented “decades of mistrust” and “competing security concerns” between Russia and Europe, vowing to address these by building an “enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” Kushner has also stressed that NATO would remain central to European defense and that no country should have a veto over another’s alliances.
Trump himself has also hinted that he seeks a final deal encompassing the entire continent. “It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” he told reporters in the Oval Office earlier this month. “I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”
Instead, the idea has been met with unease and dismay, viewed by many in Europe as echoing Putin’s hard-line war goals.
Whereas Kushner described Europe and Russia as neighbors unable to resolve their differences, the historical record shows the aggression has chiefly been directed one way. Russia seized Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022, while waging sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation against the West.
Kushner’s suggestion also touches on a central European fear: that Washington will pursue a deal at almost any cost, even if  that emboldens Putin to expand his aggression.
“Why are two real estate agents pushing this idea?” Ilves  said referring to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, another Trump envoy, both of whom made their fortunes in real estate before entering diplomacy.
“These people aren’t even diplomats,” said Ilves, who led his former Soviet republic from 2006 to 2016. “I’m not sure they have much of an idea of the long history of the development of security architecture in Europe relating to Russia.”
Asked about the criticisms, assistant White House press secretary Olivia Wales said the U.S. proposal sought to “strengthen existing European security arrangements, with NATO at their core, while developing practical mechanisms to prevent future conflict.”
Security guarantees for  Ukraine “cannot be designed without understanding the broader security framework in which they will operate,” she said in an email, adding that any final agreement must respect Europe and Ukraine’s sovereignty “and be agreed by the relevant parties.”
European officials are nonetheless unnerved by Kushner’s remarks.
Kallas, the E.U. foreign policy chief, described Russia’s maximalist war demands as “really absurd,” while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pointed out that “Europe has a security architecture — we don’t need a new one.”
Elsewhere, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the rules were not the issue: “The problem is that Russia is breaking them.” And even Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was adamant that the “security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and NATO, not by Russia.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the idea as “dangerous,” saying that European security “should not be the main agenda.”
Ukraine’s view is that Russia is in no place to make such demands, given that it’s spent more than four years failing to win the war.
“At this stage, the most Putin can negotiate is a fair ceasefire along the current line of contact,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said. And “frankly, Europe does not need a new security order; it already exists, and Russia is constantly violating it.”
Kyiv and its European backers also argue that a ceasefire must come before any peace talks, accusing Russia of stalling so it can keep bombing civilian infrastructure ahead of the frigid winter.
If Europe accepts Russia’s demands about wider continental security before there is a ceasefire, Moscow “will try to create the impression that it’s our fault that the war continues, because we don’t want to accept all their demands,” according to Sven Biscop, a director at the Egmont Institute, a Belgian think tank.
He said he believed dialogue with Russia is a good thing, a view echoed by influential Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who in an interview with the Financial Times published Tuesday said that it had been “irresponsible” to outsource talks with Putin to the U.S., which he said could be leaning toward carving up Europe into spheres of influence.
Back in Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., urged Trump’s team to refuse Putin’s demands.
The Russian leader not only wanted control of Ukraine but “he wants to redesign NATO to accommodate his revisionist ambitions,” Shaheen said, adding that any discussions about European security infrastructure should be a “nonstarter,” for the U.S. which “has benefited from the Alliance.”
Amid all of this, any substantial progress toward ending the war remains elusive.
The latest round of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week produced no major breakthrough. Kushner said Washington was working toward what could be the largest prisoner swap of the war, while reporting that Russia had agreed to give Europe a seat at the table during the next round.
Russia hasn’t quite confirmed that, instead saying that it needs “to understand from the Europeans themselves” what they can “contribute to the peace process” before allowing them to join, as Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday.
There has been some internal wrangling among the European nations about who might represent them. Leaders have agreed on a team comprising the United Kingdom (which left the E.U. in 2020), France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and European Council. Kallas herself was left off the team.
“I don’t know who among the current leaders could be a sane dialogue partner,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the state-run news agency Tass on Monday.
He likened the chosen group of European countries to “the Quartet,” a satirical poem by Russian author Ivan Krylov. In it, a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear blame their failure to form a string

articles.title_orig: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.title_zh: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.content_orig:
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design . The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini. If you have previously fed any data into Google’s AI, that’s already part of the training data. That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models. The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles. However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted. Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either. Google may use this data in other ways for up to three years—it just won’t add it to AI-training data sets.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now. Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user). Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months. So you can access that data for longer, but so can Google. The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement. Google says the change is rolling out globally, but it may take a few weeks to show up for everyone.

articles.title_orig: CA DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after Bay Area traffic incidents
articles.title_zh: CA DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after Bay Area traffic incidents
articles.content_orig:
The California Department of Motor Vehicles has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after images showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
VIDEO: Driverless Waymo tries to bypass CHP traffic break on SF freeway
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told ABC7 Eyewitness News.
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026 , Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says these new restrictions went into effect on November 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
MORE: Study finds lower crash rate for Waymo vehicles in San Francisco
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again Monday.
"I used to use it all the time and now it's like ehh I'll walk, or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: Sony defeats £2 billion UK claim over PlayStation Store pricing
articles.title_zh: Sony defeats £2 billion UK claim over PlayStation Store pricing
articles.content_orig:
Sony has defeated a major $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit over the price of PlayStation games.
The lawsuit was brought about by Alex Neill, who is representing consumers that purchased PlayStation digital content between August 2016 and February 2026. The action accused PlayStation of having a ‘near monopoly’ on digital games and add-on content on PlayStation platforms. The case argued that Sony sets strict terms and conditions on developers, and charges a 30% commission on every purchase, which results in “excessive and unfair prices”. It claimed the prices are out of proportion to the costs.
But London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected this, and said the claim failed to establish that PlayStation infringed competition law. As a result, it has dismissed the case in its entirety.
Join The Game Business Today!
The lawsuit argued that once you own a PlayStation, you are trapped within the ecosystem. The Tribunal disagreed, and ruled that Sony competes within a wider ‘systems market’ with the likes of Xbox, Nintendo and PC. It also ruled that gamers can buy physical games (at least for now).
The court said that forcing PlayStation to allow third-party stores onto the platform would be expensive, complex and could impact security. It added that under competition law, there was no legal duty for Sony to do this.
Finally, the court didn’t find pricing to be unfair. It said that Alex Neill had failed to prove Sony’s profit margins were excessive, especially as console makers sell hardware cheaply to make money back on game sales. Furthermore, there tribunal said there no evidence that rival stores would have brought pricing down.
PlayStation still faces similar class actions in Australia, Netherlands and Portugal at an earlier stage.
For more details on the Alex Neill case, you can read our run-down from earlier this year.
The Game Business is a reader-supported publication. Join us today!
Sony's digital store has always charged significantly more than physical stores, despite digital obviously having lower production costs/overheads.
Forcing Sony to allow alternate stores isn't the answer but forcing Sony to allow retailers to sell digital codes would have been a fair compromise, potentially recreating the pre-digital dynamic.
Not only would this result in positive pricing competition, it might allow the games retail scene to grow again, and help sustain nice shops/third spaces for gamers to come together rather than it all be done online.
Perhaps current competition law isn't equipped to deal with the digital age and needs to be reviewed?

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Deutsche Bank Leak Exposes Epstein Payments—Democrats Could Hold It And Other Banks Accountable
articles.title_zh: Deutsche Bank Leak Exposes Epstein Payments—Democrats Could Hold It And Other Banks Accountable
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.
These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump 's tax statements.
The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.
Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower by 9:20 a.m. E.T., having fallen more than 6% in early trade in Frankfurt.
Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported . Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.
The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.
The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.
It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.
The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife.
The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny.
The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years.
"Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.
The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025.
"Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."
CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

articles.title_orig: Hacker Who Leaked Grand Theft Auto VI Clips Pleads Guilty to Cybercrimes
articles.title_zh: Hacker Who Leaked Grand Theft Auto VI Clips Pleads Guilty to Cybercrimes
articles.content_orig:
A hacker has pleaded guilty to a string of online crimes, including trying to extort the makers of Grand Theft Auto 6 after stealing dozens of unfinished clips of the game.
21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, carried out the hack in 2022, and was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.
But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.
On Monday, Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
Kurtaj breached Rockstar Games in 2022 whilst he was on bail for multiple other hacking offences and under police protection.
He was being housed in a Travelodge in Bicester to protect him from rival hackers who threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.
With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."
The company refused to cooperate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.
Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.79m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.
The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.
At the time, doctors deemed Kurtaj unfit to stand in a traditional trial due to the severity of his autism, so instead he was given what is known as a trial of the facts.
The jury was asked to determine whether or not he committed the alleged acts - not if he did so with criminal intent.
In December 2023 the court ruled that he would remain at a secure hospital for life unless doctors deem him no longer a danger.
A routine assessment late last year deemed that he was now fit to stand a criminal trial which was scheduled to take place at Woolwich Crown Court.
But Kurtaj pleaded guilty to all offences.
He sat in the dock with short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt but no tie.
The now 21-year-old blinked frequently during the hearing and stood to confirm his name, and pled guilty to all counts with no visible emotion.
Those included hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber where he used social engineering techniques to gain access to internal systems.
The court heard that during his hack on Uber he posted a picture of a penis as part of his attempts to force the company to pay a ransom.
His hacks on the companies are estimated to have caused around £10m of damage.
Using the data stolen from the firms, he and other members of the gang targeted cryptocurrency investors.
The prosecution argued that the gang stole at least $300,000 from individual victims.
Kurtaj also pleaded guilty to physical assaults on workers whilst in custody including multiple biting incidents.
Whilst in prison he was caught with a mobile phone after sending a taunting text message to police and posting updates on Snapchat.
Kurtaj will be sentenced at a later date.
In the 2023 original trial, another Lapsus$ member, who was 17, was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court.
The 17-year-old, who could not be named at the time due to his age, was sentenced to an 18-month Youth Rehabilitation Order, including intense supervision and a ban on using VPNs online.
Earlier this year that same hacker, now named as Thalha Jubair, was jailed for five years and six months after continuing his cyber crime offences with another group known as Scattered Spider.
Amongst victims was Transport for London which was subjected to a disruptive cyber attack that caused around £39m of damage and caused chaos inside the firm.

articles.title_orig: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.title_zh: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.content_orig:
The Civilization and XCOM developer is shrinking as a new XCOM game has missed a development milestone, according to Bloomberg
Take-Two Interactive $TTWO 's Firaxis Games cut roughly 60 jobs on Tuesday, about one-third of the studio's workforce, according to Bloomberg .
A spokesperson from 2K Games, the Take-Two imprint that oversees Firaxis, verified that Heather Hazen, who heads the studio, is departing, according to Bloomberg. The Maryland-based studio makes the Civilization and XCOM franchises.
"Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength — designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years," the spokesperson said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. "As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis."
The spokesperson described Hazen’s exit as a planned handover, according to Game Developer . “With the studio entering this reset, she feels this is the right, deliberate moment to hand over the reins to ensure the next studio leader has full ownership of this new era from the start,” the spokesperson said, according to Game Developer.
Firaxis has been working on a new XCOM title that ran into development problems and fell short of an important milestone this summer, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg, citing unnamed people, said work on the game will go on, though the cuts could bring major changes to it.
“Civilization VII,” the studio’s latest title, came out last year to a lukewarm response and has been patched repeatedly since, according to Bloomberg. The game holds a 51% positive user rating on Steam, according to Kotaku .
The layoffs land just two days prior to “Grand Theft Auto VI” hitting the market, according to Bloomberg. Rockstar, a separate Take-Two label, develops and publishes that game.
